Brand names that became everyday words.Escalator: Otis trademarked the name in 1900, but a court ruled it generic in 1950 and so anyone could call a moving staircase one.
Brand names that became everyday words.Thermos: Named from the Greek for heat, the name was lost as a trademark in the US in 1963 when a court decided it had become a common word.
Brand names that became everyday words.Band-Aid: Earle Dickson, a Johnson & Johnson employee, invented it for his accident-prone wife, who kept cutting herself in the kitchen.
Brand names that became everyday words.Kleenex: Introduced as a cold-cream remover for makeup, it only later became known as a disposable handkerchief.
Brand names that became everyday words.Sellotape: Its name is a nod to cellophane, and in Britain, Australia and elsewhere it became the everyday word for clear sticky tape.
Brand names that became everyday words.Velcro: Engineer George de Mestral invented it after burrs clung to his dog's fur on an Alpine walk; the name blends velours and crochet.
Brand names that became everyday words.Frisbee: Named for the Frisbie Pie Company of Connecticut, whose empty tins college students sent flying across campuses.
Brand names that became everyday words.Jacuzzi: The Jacuzzi brothers first made a pump to ease a family member's arthritis; the whirlpool bath followed later.
Brand names that became everyday words.Jet Ski: Kawasaki's trademark for personal watercraft is still used by many people for any stand-up or sit-down water scooter.
Brand names that became everyday words.Google: It started as a play on googol, the number 1 followed by 100 zeros, and it became an official dictionary verb in 2006.

When these cities got their metro or sub.Chicago 'L': The world's first elevated rail in the 1890s gave downtown its name, the Loop, and it still runs both elevated and underground.
When these cities got their metro or sub.Glasgow: It is called the Clockwork Orange for its orange trains, and is the world's third-oldest underground after London and Budapest.
When these cities got their metro or sub.Madrid: King Alfonso XIII opened it, and it has since grown into one of the largest metro networks in the world.
When these cities got their metro or sub.Barcelona: Its first line, Gran Metro, linked Lesseps and Catalunya.
When these cities got their metro or sub.Stockholm: Its rock-hewn stations are decorated with art, earning it the nickname world's longest art gallery.
When these cities got their metro or sub.Toronto: It was Canada's first subway, running under Yonge Street.
When these cities got their metro or sub.Montreal: It runs on rubber tires and each station was designed by a different architect.
When these cities got their metro or sub.San Francisco BART: Its Transbay Tube runs under San Francisco Bay for about six kilometers.
When these cities got their metro or sub.Singapore: Eating and drinking are banned in the stations, and it is famous for being spotless.
When these cities got their metro or sub.Dubai: It is a driverless network that was among the longest of its kind when it opened.

When these words were coined.Yahoo: Swift used it in Gulliver's Travels for brutish human-like creatures; the search engine later claimed it stood for Yet Another Hierarchical Officious Oracle.
When these words were coined.Serendipity: Horace Walpole coined it from a fairy tale, The Three Princes of Serendip, whose heroes keep finding things by accident.
When these words were coined.Chortle: Lewis Carroll blended chuckle and snort in Through the Looking-Glass in 1871.
When these words were coined.Robot: Karel Capek's play R.U.R. introduced it, from the Czech robota for forced labour; he credited his brother Josef with the word.
When these words were coined.Nerd: Dr. Seuss used it in If I Ran the Zoo as the name of a grumpy creature; the modern meaning came later.
When these words were coined.Meme: Richard Dawkins coined it in The Selfish Gene as a cultural analogue of a gene.
When these words were coined.Cyberspace: William Gibson coined it in his 1982 story Burning Chrome and popularised it in Neuromancer.
When these words were coined.Muggle: Rowling coined it in Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone, and it is now in the Oxford English Dictionary.
When these words were coined.Truthiness: Stephen Colbert coined it on the first Colbert Report episode, and the American Dialect Society named it word of 2005.
When these words were coined.Covfefe: A midnight tweet in May 2017 left this typo hanging, and it became a viral joke worldwide.

Fast, faster, fastest.Fastest tennis serve: Sam Groth's 2012 serve at a Challenger event in Busan, South Korea, is the fastest ever recorded.
Fast, faster, fastest.Formula 1 car (record): F1 cars brake from over 300 km/h to a near stop in a few seconds, pulling about five times gravity.
Fast, faster, fastest.Airliner cruising: Covering a kilometre every four seconds, airliners can fly faster by riding the jet stream.
Fast, faster, fastest.Speed of sound: Thunder arrives about three seconds per kilometre after a lightning flash, because sound is so much slower than light.
Fast, faster, fastest.Concorde: Friction heated its skin above 100 degrees, and the aircraft stretched by several inches in flight.
Fast, faster, fastest.Rifle bullet: Many bullets leave the muzzle faster than sound, so the crack of its shock wave comes through before the report.
Fast, faster, fastest.International Space Station: The station laps Earth about every 90 minutes, so astronauts see about 16 sunrises and sunsets a day.
Fast, faster, fastest.Earth orbiting the Sun: Earth moves at roughly 30 km per second around the Sun, and the whole solar system also orbits the galaxy's centre.
Fast, faster, fastest.Parker Solar Probe: In December 2024 it flew closest to the Sun and became the fastest human-made object.
Fast, faster, fastest.Light: Light covers 300,000 km a second, and nothing with mass can reach it.

Kitchen and bar measures.US teaspoon: A US teaspoon is a bit under 5 ml, and nutrition labels round it to exactly 5 ml for convenience.
Kitchen and bar measures.US tablespoon: A tablespoon equals three teaspoons, and in Australia it is bigger, at 20 ml.
Kitchen and bar measures.US fluid ounce: This measure is just under 30 ml, and it differs slightly from its British version, which is about 28 ml.
Kitchen and bar measures.Jigger: This two-sided metal cup helps bartenders pour a measure of a spirit, and in the US it's 1.5 fluid ounces.
Kitchen and bar measures.US cup: A US cup is about 237 ml, and metric cooks often use a round 250 ml cup instead.
Kitchen and bar measures.US pint: The US version of this is 16 fluid ounces, and a smaller one than the British pint, so American beer drinkers get less.
Kitchen and bar measures.Imperial (UK) pint: This pub measure is 20 imperial fluid ounces, and by law the pub pint in the UK must be this size.
Kitchen and bar measures.US quart: A quart means a quarter of a gallon, and the word comes from the Latin for 'fourth'.
Kitchen and bar measures.US gallon: The US version is 128 fluid ounces, and a gallon of milk is a common sight in American fridges.
Kitchen and bar measures.Imperial gallon: The British gallon is about 20 percent larger than the American one, so fuel economy numbers in miles per gallon differ across the Atlantic.

From freezer to pizza oven: kitchen temp.Home freezer: Freezers sit at -18°C because bacteria and molds can't grow there, though food still slowly loses flavor and texture over the months.
From freezer to pizza oven: kitchen temp.Fridge: Below about 4°C bacterial growth slows sharply, which is why leftovers last days in the fridge but only hours on a warm counter.
From freezer to pizza oven: kitchen temp.Tempered dark chocolate: Tempering melts and carefully cools chocolate to form stable cocoa butter crystals, giving the glossy shine and the clean snap.
From freezer to pizza oven: kitchen temp.Rare steak, at the center: A rare steak stays red and juicy because its muscle proteins have only begun to firm up, so the center is warm rather than truly cooked.
From freezer to pizza oven: kitchen temp.Safely cooked chicken: The 74°C target is a safety number: Salmonella dies almost instantly at that heat, though lower temperatures work too if held longer.
From freezer to pizza oven: kitchen temp.Boiling water at sea level: Water only boils at 100°C at sea level; on top of Mount Everest it boils at roughly 70°C, which makes for a feeble cup of tea.
From freezer to pizza oven: kitchen temp.Inside a pressure cooker: Sealed-in steam raises the pressure, so water boils well above 100°C inside and tough beans and cuts of meat soften in a fraction of the time.
From freezer to pizza oven: kitchen temp.Deep-frying oil: At this heat the food's surface moisture flashes to steam, pushing outward and keeping oil from soaking in, which is what makes fried food crisp.
From freezer to pizza oven: kitchen temp.Oven for crusty bread: Early steam in a hot oven keeps the crust stretchy so the loaf can balloon, called oven spring, before the surface sets into a crackling shell.
From freezer to pizza oven: kitchen temp.Neapolitan pizza oven: The art of Neapolitan pizza-making is UNESCO-listed, and a wood-fired dome this hot bakes a pie in only about 60 to 90 seconds.

Round things by diameter.US penny: Since 1982 the US penny has been mostly zinc with only a thin copper plating, because copper became worth more than a cent.
Round things by diameter.US quarter: The quarter's edge has 119 ridges, a holdover from when edges of silver coins deterred people from shaving off a little metal.
Round things by diameter.Golf ball: A regulation golf ball has roughly 300 to 500 dimples that cut drag and create lift, so it flies much farther than a smooth one would.
Round things by diameter.Tennis ball: Wimbledon switched to yellow balls only in 1986, because they showed up better on television than white ones.
Round things by diameter.Compact disc: The size is often said to have been set so one disc could hold Beethoven's Ninth Symphony, giving about 74 minutes of music.
Round things by diameter.Ultimate frisbee: The Frisbee name comes from the Frisbie Pie Company of Connecticut, whose empty pie tins students are said to have tossed around.
Round things by diameter.Basketball rim: The rim sits 10 feet up because James Naismith nailed peach baskets to a gym balcony in 1891, and the height simply stuck.
Round things by diameter.Manhole cover: Manhole covers are round because a round lid can never fall through its own opening, unlike a square one, which can slip in diagonally.
Round things by diameter.Road bike wheel: Most road bike wheels are labeled 700c, a leftover French sizing code that no longer matches any real measurement.
Round things by diameter.London Eye: Built for the millennium and meant to be temporary, it proved so popular that it became permanent and was the world's tallest Ferris wheel when it opened.

Epic poems, by number of lines.Gawain and the Green Knight: Its anonymous poet probably also wrote Pearl, and it is written in alliterative Middle English, a rhythm unlike modern verse.
Epic poems, by number of lines.Beowulf: Only one manuscript survives, damaged by fire in 1731, and Tolkien's 1936 lecture helped make people see it as literature.
Epic poems, by number of lines.The Song of Roland: The Roncevaux battle it recounts was real, but in 778, against Basques rather than the Muslim army the poem describes.
Epic poems, by number of lines.The Aeneid: Virgil asked on his deathbed to have it burned, but Emperor Augustus overruled him, so Rome's national epic survived.
Epic poems, by number of lines.Paradise Lost: Milton dictated it after going blind, and at its start he promises to justify the ways of God to men.
Epic poems, by number of lines.The Odyssey: It opens in the middle of the story, with Odysseus already stranded on Calypso's island after most of his journey.
Epic poems, by number of lines.The Divine Comedy: Dante wrote it in terza rima, interlocking three-line stanzas, and chose Tuscan Italian instead of Latin, helping to shape the language.
Epic poems, by number of lines.The Iliad: It covers only a few weeks of the ten-year Trojan War, and does not even include the wooden horse.
Epic poems, by number of lines.The Faerie Queene: Spenser wrote it to honor Elizabeth I, and it was left unfinished, with only six of the twelve planned books.
Epic poems, by number of lines.The Mahabharata: About ten times as long as the Iliad and Odyssey combined, it includes the Bhagavad Gita as one section.

One big album for each year of the 2000s.Kid A: Radiohead embraced electronic sounds and left out singles, a bold move that left many fans puzzled at first.
One big album for each year of the 2000s.Discovery (Daft Punk): Daft Punk's disco-house album inspired an anime film, Interstella 5555, which has no dialogue and uses the album as its soundtrack.
One big album for each year of the 2000s.A Rush of Blood to the Head: Coldplay's second album includes 'Clocks', and its piano riff became one of the most recognizable of the decade.
One big album for each year of the 2000s.Elephant (The White Stripes): Recorded in about two weeks in London with vintage gear, it includes 'Seven Nation Army', a stadium chant everywhere.
One big album for each year of the 2000s.American Idiot: Green Day's rock opera about a suburban outsider was later turned into a Broadway musical.
One big album for each year of the 2000s.Late Registration: Kanye West worked with producer Jon Brion on this orchestral-leaning album, which won the Grammy for Best Rap Album.
One big album for each year of the 2000s.FutureSex/LoveSounds: Justin Timberlake teamed with producer Timbaland on this follow-up, which includes 'SexyBack' and a dense electro-pop sound.
One big album for each year of the 2000s.In Rainbows: Radiohead let fans pay whatever they wanted when it was first released for download, a famous experiment.
One big album for each year of the 2000s.Viva la Vida: Named for a Frida Kahlo painting, it was produced with Brian Eno and won the Grammy for Best Rock Album.
One big album for each year of the 2000s.The Fame Monster: This extended edition included 'Bad Romance', a huge hit for Lady Gaga with a Hitchcock-inspired music video.

Golf scores on a single hole.Ostrich: Practically never achieved, it would take a hole-in-one on a par 6.
Golf scores on a single hole.Condor: A hole-in-one on a par 5 earns this, and only a handful have ever been recorded.
Golf scores on a single hole.Albatross: Called a double eagle in the US; Gene Sarazen's shot at the 1935 Masters is the most famous.
Golf scores on a single hole.Eagle: After birdie, golfers needed a bigger bird name, and eagle won.
Golf scores on a single hole.Birdie: The term was coined in Atlantic City around 1899 for an excellent shot, 'a bird of a shot'.
Golf scores on a single hole.Par: The word means equal in Latin, borrowed from stock-market talk like par value.
Golf scores on a single hole.Bogey: Originally the score a good player was expected to make, named for a mythical 'Colonel Bogey'.
Golf scores on a single hole.Double bogey: On a par 4 it means a six, a typical amateur result on a tough hole.
Golf scores on a single hole.Triple bogey: On a par 4 it means a seven, and hazards or lost balls usually cause it.
Golf scores on a single hole.Quadruple bogey: Jordan Spieth took a seven on a par 3 at the 2016 Masters, which cost him the title.

Whales and dolphins by weight.Harbor porpoise: This small, shy porpoise lives in cool coastal waters and surfaces so quietly that it is easily missed. It has a blunt face, unlike a dolphin's beak.
Whales and dolphins by weight.Common dolphin: These are among the most numerous and sociable dolphins, sometimes gathering in groups of hundreds or even thousands, and they love riding bow waves.
Whales and dolphins by weight.Bottlenose dolphin: The species of most aquariums and films, it can hold its breath for several minutes and talks using clicks and whistles, including signature whistles that act like names.
Whales and dolphins by weight.Risso's dolphin: Also called the grampus, it is easy to spot because its gray skin becomes covered in white scars from encounters with others of its kind and with squid.
Whales and dolphins by weight.Beluga: The white "canary of the sea" is named for its chirps and whistles. It is one of few whales whose neck can bend and whose face can change shape.
Whales and dolphins by weight.Minke whale: Minkes are the smallest of the baleen rorquals, yet one is still heavier than several cars. They are curious and sometimes approach boats.
Whales and dolphins by weight.Humpback whale: Males compose complex songs that last up to about 20 minutes and can spread through whole populations, changing gradually over the years.
Whales and dolphins by weight.Sperm whale (male): Its head holds the spermaceti organ, and it dives more than 1,000 metres to hunt giant squid. Its brain is the largest of any animal.
Whales and dolphins by weight.Fin whale: The second-largest animal ever is also fast for its size, reaching about 37 km/h in bursts, which earned it the nickname "greyhound of the sea".
Whales and dolphins by weight.Blue whale: The largest animal known ever to have lived. Its calls are among the loudest of any animal and can travel for hundreds of kilometers underwater.

Guess the weight: ten very different ani.Monarch butterfly: A monarch weighs about as much as a paperclip, yet it can migrate thousands of kilometers to Mexico.
Guess the weight: ten very different ani.Common frog: A common frog breathes partly through its skin, and it can absorb water without drinking.
Guess the weight: ten very different ani.Platypus: The platypus lays eggs, and males carry a venomous spur on each hind leg.
Guess the weight: ten very different ani.Canada goose: A Canada goose flies in V formation, which lets birds save energy by riding each other's air flow.
Guess the weight: ten very different ani.Emperor penguin: Emperor penguins huddle together through the Antarctic winter, while males balance a single egg on their feet for about two months.
Guess the weight: ten very different ani.Red kangaroo: A red kangaroo can bound about 8 meters in a single leap and is the largest marsupial.
Guess the weight: ten very different ani.Grizzly bear: A grizzly can run at about 55 km/h, which is faster than any human sprinter.
Guess the weight: ten very different ani.American bison: The American bison nearly went extinct in the 1880s, with only a few hundred left in the wild.
Guess the weight: ten very different ani.White rhino: The white rhino's name probably comes from an Afrikaans word meaning wide, referring to its mouth, not its color.
Guess the weight: ten very different ani.Humpback whale: Humpback whales sing long songs that can be heard across much of an ocean, and males in a population share the same song.

When these indie games came out.Cave Story: Daisuke Amaya made it alone over about five years, as free software, and it helped inspire the modern indie boom.
When these indie games came out.Braid: Jonathan Blow's puzzle platformer lets you rewind time, and its success on Xbox Live Arcade proved small games could be hits.
When these indie games came out.Super Meat Boy: Its brutally hard levels and a tiny cube hero were featured in the documentary Indie Game: The Movie.
When these indie games came out.Terraria: Often called '2D Minecraft', the digging-and-building adventure has sold tens of millions of copies.
When these indie games came out.Papers, Please: Lucas Pope's game makes you a border inspector in the made-up state of Arstotzka, with a moral dilemma in every stamp.
When these indie games came out.Undertale: Toby Fox funded it on Kickstarter, and it can be completed without killing anyone, a choice the game remarks upon.
When these indie games came out.Stardew Valley: Eric Barone made it almost entirely alone over about four years, inspired by the farming game Harvest Moon.
When these indie games came out.Celeste: A mountain-climbing platformer that deals with anxiety, it included an assist mode so players could tune the difficulty.
When these indie games came out.Hades: After more than a year in early access, its 1.0 launch won huge praise, and it took the Hugo Award for best video game.
When these indie games came out.Balatro: A poker-based roguelike made by a developer known only as LocalThunk, it became a surprise smash hit.

When these 'Greats' came to power.Sargon the Great: He founded Akkad, often called the first empire, and legend says he was found as a baby in a basket on a river.
When these 'Greats' came to power.Cyrus the Great: He founded the Persian Empire, and is said to have freed the exiles in Babylon. The Cyrus Cylinder records his policy of tolerance.
When these 'Greats' came to power.Alexander the Great: He took the throne at 20, was tutored by Aristotle, and never lost a battle before dying in Babylon at 32.
When these 'Greats' came to power.Ashoka the Great: This Indian emperor turned to Buddhism after a bloody war, then spread his message through edicts carved on stone pillars.
When these 'Greats' came to power.Constantine the Great: He was proclaimed emperor in York, legalised Christianity across the empire, and founded Constantinople as his capital.
When these 'Greats' came to power.Theodoric the Great: The Ostrogoth king grew up as a hostage in Constantinople, then ruled Italy from Ravenna with Roman-style government.
When these 'Greats' came to power.Charles the Great: Known as Charlemagne, he was crowned emperor on Christmas Day, 800, and is sometimes called the 'father of Europe'.
When these 'Greats' came to power.Alfred the Great: The only English monarch called 'the Great', he held off the Vikings, and legend says he once burned some cakes.
When these 'Greats' came to power.Otto the Great: After he defeated the Magyars in 955, he was crowned emperor in 962, which is considered the start of the Holy Roman Empire.
When these 'Greats' came to power.Casimir the Great: Poland's king reportedly left it 'of stone' after finding it 'of wood', and founded the University of Kraków in 1364.

World Cups in nations that hosted only o.Uruguay: The first World Cup was played in Montevideo, and the host country won it, beating Argentina in the final. Only 13 teams took part.
World Cups in nations that hosted only o.Switzerland: This was the highest-scoring World Cup ever, with 5.38 goals per game, and Hungary was beaten in the final in the 'Miracle of Bern'.
World Cups in nations that hosted only o.Sweden: A 17-year-old Pelé burst onto the world stage here, scoring twice in the final and helping Brazil win its first title.
World Cups in nations that hosted only o.Chile: Brazil won again without Pelé, who was injured early on, and the tournament was marred by violent matches like the 'Battle of Santiago'.
World Cups in nations that hosted only o.England: England's only win came in this tournament, with Geoff Hurst's hat-trick in the final and the stolen trophy found by a dog named Pickles.
World Cups in nations that hosted only o.Argentina: Argentina won its first title on home soil, beating the Netherlands in extra time, amid controversy as the country was under military rule.
World Cups in nations that hosted only o.Spain: Spain staged the first 24-team tournament, and the mascot Naranjito was an orange with a smiling face.
World Cups in nations that hosted only o.Japan and South Korea: It was the first World Cup held in Asia and the first with two hosts, and Brazil beat Germany in the final for its fifth title.
World Cups in nations that hosted only o.South Africa: The first one on the African continent was famous for the buzzing vuvuzela horns, and Spain won its first title.
World Cups in nations that hosted only o.Russia: This tournament was held in 11 cities in Europe and France won its second title, beating Croatia 4-2 in the final.

Mathematical firsts by value.Smallest prime: It is the only even prime number, which makes it the oddest prime, so to speak.
Mathematical firsts by value.Smallest odd prime: The number of dimensions we move in, and the smallest number of sides a polygon can have.
Mathematical firsts by value.Smallest perfect number: It is perfect because its divisors 1, 2 and 3 add up to 6, and perfect numbers are very rare.
Mathematical firsts by value.Smallest two-digit prime: It is the only palindromic prime with an even number of digits, since all other even-length palindromes divide by 11.
Mathematical firsts by value.Smallest two-digit square: It is 4 squared and also 2 to the fourth power, the only pair of different whole numbers with a^b = b^a.
Mathematical firsts by value.Second perfect number: A perfect number, since its divisors 1, 2, 4, 7 and 14 add up to 28, and also the days of a short February.
Mathematical firsts by value.Smallest divisible by 1 to 6: The smallest number divisible by 1 through 6, and Babylonian base 60 is why we still have 60 minutes and 60 seconds.
Mathematical firsts by value.Smallest three-digit prime: A palindromic prime, and Room 101 is the dreaded torture room in Nineteen Eighty-Four.
Mathematical firsts by value.Smallest four-digit prime: The first four-digit prime, since every number from 1,000 to 1,008 is composite, and 1,001 is 7 times 11 times 13.
Mathematical firsts by value.Smallest four-digit square: It is 32 squared and 2 to the tenth power, which is why a kilobyte was long counted as 1,024 bytes.

French Revolutionary calendar months, in.Vendémiaire: Its name comes from the Latin for the grape harvest, and this month began around 22 September.
French Revolutionary calendar months, in.Brumaire: Napoleon's 1799 coup took place on the 18th of this month, which is why it is still how the coup is remembered.
French Revolutionary calendar months, in.Frimaire: The name comes from the French word frimas, meaning frost.
French Revolutionary calendar months, in.Nivôse: The name comes from the Latin nivosus, meaning snowy, and the month ran from December into January.
French Revolutionary calendar months, in.Ventôse: The names were invented by the poet Fabre d'Églantine, who tied each one to the weather or the harvest.
French Revolutionary calendar months, in.Germinal: Zola borrowed the name for his 1885 novel Germinal, set among coal miners.
French Revolutionary calendar months, in.Floréal: It ran from late April into May, when the fields flower.
French Revolutionary calendar months, in.Messidor: The name comes from the Latin messis, meaning harvest, in early summer.
French Revolutionary calendar months, in.Thermidor: Robespierre fell on the ninth of this month in 1794, so the word still stands for the end of a revolution's radical phase.
French Revolutionary calendar months, in.Fructidor: The year ended with this month, followed by five or six extra days at the end of the year.

How long these old walls are.Roman walls of Lugo: Lugo's walls are the only fully intact Roman city walls in the world, and they are UNESCO listed.
How long these old walls are.York city walls: York has the longest medieval walls in England, and you can walk almost all the way around them.
How long these old walls are.Theodosian Land Walls: They protected Constantinople for about a thousand years, until cannons helped the Ottomans break through in 1453.
How long these old walls are.Servian Wall, Rome: Rome built it after the Gauls sacked the city in 390 BC, and later tradition credited King Servius Tullius.
How long these old walls are.Aurelian Walls, Rome: Built in the 270s AD, most of it still stands, and it was the city's defence into the 19th century.
How long these old walls are.Kumbhalgarh Fort wall: Wide enough for horses to ride side by side, it is the longest continuous wall after the Great Wall of China.
How long these old walls are.Antonine Wall: It ran from the Firth of Forth to the Clyde and was abandoned within a couple of decades.
How long these old walls are.Hadrian's Wall: Eighty Roman miles long, it has milecastles along the way, and it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
How long these old walls are.Great Wall of Gorgan: Known as the Red Snake, it was Sasanian Persia's frontier defence, with dozens of forts.
How long these old walls are.Great Wall of China: It is not visible to the naked eye from space, and it was built in many sections by different dynasties over centuries.

Chinese festivals through the lunar year.Spring Festival: The Chinese New Year, centered on family reunions, red envelopes and fireworks, is the biggest holiday of the lunar year and sparks a huge annual migration.
Chinese festivals through the lunar year.Lantern Festival: It falls on the first full moon after New Year, and people eat tangyuan, sweet glutinous rice balls, and solve riddles on lanterns.
Chinese festivals through the lunar year.Dragon Raises Its Head: This day marks the dragon lifting its head, so that rains come, and some people get haircuts for luck.
Chinese festivals through the lunar year.Dragon Boat Festival: Boat races on rivers and sticky rice dumplings, zongzi, honor the poet Qu Yuan, who is said to have drowned himself.
Chinese festivals through the lunar year.Qixi lovers festival: Based on a legend of a weaver girl and a cowherd who can only meet once a year on a bridge of magpies, it is China's Valentine's Day.
Chinese festivals through the lunar year.Ghost Festival: People burn paper offerings and food for wandering spirits, and the gates of the underworld are said to open.
Chinese festivals through the lunar year.Mid-Autumn Festival: Families gather to admire the full moon and eat mooncakes, and the story of the Moon goddess Chang'e is told.
Chinese festivals through the lunar year.Double Ninth Festival: The date has two nines, a lucky number meaning long life, so people climb hills and drink chrysanthemum wine.
Chinese festivals through the lunar year.Laba Festival: A bowl of sweet porridge with grains and beans is eaten, and this day in Buddhist tradition marks the Buddha's enlightenment.
Chinese festivals through the lunar year.Kitchen God Festival: People offer sweets to the kitchen god, so he'll report good things about the family to the Jade Emperor.

Count the sides (or panels).Yield sign: Its inverted triangle is unique among road signs, so it is recognizable even from behind.
Count the sides (or panels).Baseball diamond: The 'diamond' is really a square, with 90 feet between bases, turned onto a corner.
Count the sides (or panels).Baseball home plate: Its five-sided shape replaced a square plate around 1900, and helps umpires judge the strike zone.
Count the sides (or panels).Hex nut: Six sides let a wrench grip from many angles in tight spaces.
Count the sides (or panels).UK 50p coin: Britain's 50p has seven curved sides, so it rolls like a round coin in machines yet is easy to tell by touch.
Count the sides (or panels).Stop sign: In the US, stop signs were yellow until the 1950s; the red octagon is recognizable from behind or under snow.
Count the sides (or panels).Canadian loonie coin: Canada's dollar coin has 11 sides and is nicknamed for the loon on its back, in use since 1987.
Count the sides (or panels).Australian 50-cent coin: Australia's 50-cent coin has 12 sides, and is one of the world's largest coins in circulation.
Count the sides (or panels).Icosahedron (faces): It has 20 triangular faces; Dungeons & Dragons players roll it as the d20.
Count the sides (or panels).Classic soccer ball (panels): The classic black-and-white design is a truncated icosahedron, 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons, a shape chemists later found in buckyballs.

Human heights, from tiny to towering.Newborn baby: Babies are born with around 300 bones that fuse into the 206 of an adult, and they gain about half again their length in the first year.
Human heights, from tiny to towering.Jyoti Amge: Guinness lists her as the shortest living woman, at about 63 cm, and she appeared on American Horror Story.
Human heights, from tiny to towering.Typical 10-year-old: Girls often hit their growth spurt earlier than boys, so at this age they are on average a bit taller.
Human heights, from tiny to towering.Average US woman: Average heights have grown over the past century in most countries, with the Dutch now among the tallest.
Human heights, from tiny to towering.Average US man: Americans were among the tallest people in the 19th century, but the Dutch have since passed them.
Human heights, from tiny to towering.Michael Jordan: Famously cut from his high school varsity team as a sophomore, he later won six NBA titles, and 6 foot 6 was tall but not the biggest in the league.
Human heights, from tiny to towering.Shaquille O'Neal: The big center wore size 22 shoes, and he towered over most opponents, including at the free-throw line.
Human heights, from tiny to towering.Yao Ming: The Chinese center was the first overall NBA draft pick in 2002 and became an icon in both China and the US.
Human heights, from tiny to towering.Sultan Kösen: The Turkish farmer is listed by Guinness as the tallest living man; his height comes from a pituitary tumor that doctors later treated.
Human heights, from tiny to towering.Robert Wadlow: The man from Alton, Illinois, is the tallest person in recorded history, at about 8 feet 11 inches, and still growing when he died at 22.

Milestones in childbirth medicine.Obstetric forceps: The Chamberlen family of surgeons kept their design a secret for generations and hid it under a sheet while working.
Milestones in childbirth medicine.Semmelweis: wash your hands: Handwashing in chlorinated lime cut deaths from childbed fever in his Vienna ward, but his colleagues rejected the idea.
Milestones in childbirth medicine.Chloroform for Queen Victoria: Her use of anaesthesia, given by John Snow for the birth of Prince Leopold, helped make pain relief in labor respectable.
Milestones in childbirth medicine.Tarnier's baby incubator: The French doctor drew on poultry incubators he saw at a zoo, and his device cut deaths among premature babies.
Milestones in childbirth medicine.Apgar score: Virginia Apgar's quick score of five signs at one and five minutes after birth is still used worldwide.
Milestones in childbirth medicine.Pregnancy ultrasound: Ian Donald in Glasgow adapted a technique used for finding flaws in ships' metal to look at unborn babies.
Milestones in childbirth medicine.The contraceptive pill: Approved in the US in 1960, it was among the first drugs taken by healthy people and changed family planning.
Milestones in childbirth medicine.Newborn heel-prick test: Robert Guthrie's test was first aimed at PKU, a metabolic disorder that is harmless when found early, and screening now covers dozens of conditions.
Milestones in childbirth medicine.Anti-D injection: It stops Rh-negative mothers from forming antibodies against later Rh-positive babies, a once deadly problem.
Milestones in childbirth medicine.First IVF baby: Louise Brown was born in Oldham, and Robert Edwards received a Nobel Prize for the technique in 2010.

Cricket by the numbers.Bails on a wicket: Two small wooden crosspieces rest on the stumps and must be dislodged to be bowled out; some now light up.
Cricket by the numbers.Stumps in a wicket: Three upright stakes about 71 cm tall; a delivery that hits them means the batter is bowled.
Cricket by the numbers.Runs for a boundary four: The ball must cross the boundary rope after touching the ground to count four; clearing it scores six.
Cricket by the numbers.Balls in an over: Australia once used eight-ball overs until 1979-80, with most of the rest of the world on six.
Cricket by the numbers.Players per side: Eleven players a side, plus substitute fielders who can't bat or bowl.
Cricket by the numbers.Overs per side in a T20: Introduced by England's cricket board in 2003, it made matches short enough to finish in about three hours.
Cricket by the numbers.Yards between the wickets: A chain, 22 yards, was a surveyor's unit, and the pitch length derives from it.
Cricket by the numbers.Overs per side in an ODI: The first one-day international was improvised in Melbourne in 1971 after a Test match washed out.
Cricket by the numbers.Minimum overs in a Test day: A Test day is scheduled for at least 90 overs, in about six hours of play.
Cricket by the numbers.Balls per innings, The Hundred: England's 2021 competition shortens the game to 100 balls per side, bowled in sets of five or ten.

SI prefixes, including the 2022 newcomer.quecto-: Added in 2022, its symbol q was free; an electron weighs about 910 quectograms.
SI prefixes, including the 2022 newcomer.ronto-: One of four prefixes added in 2022, the first new ones since 1991, to keep up with the data and science of ever-tinier things.
SI prefixes, including the 2022 newcomer.femto-: From the Danish word for fifteen; femtosecond laser pulses let chemists watch chemical bonds break and form.
SI prefixes, including the 2022 newcomer.micro-: From Greek for 'small'; a human hair is roughly 70 micrometres thick.
SI prefixes, including the 2022 newcomer.centi-: From Latin for 'hundred', it survives mainly in the centimetre and little else in everyday measuring.
SI prefixes, including the 2022 newcomer.hecto-: From the Greek for hundred; you meet it in hectares and in hectopascals on weather maps.
SI prefixes, including the 2022 newcomer.mega-: From Greek for 'great', it is why a megawatt can power hundreds of homes and a megaphone shouts so loudly.
SI prefixes, including the 2022 newcomer.exa-: Taken from the Greek word for six, since it is 1,000 to the sixth power; your phone's storage will not reach it any time soon.
SI prefixes, including the 2022 newcomer.ronna-: Earth's mass is about six ronnagrams, which is why the prefix was invented for planets and not for kitchen scales.
SI prefixes, including the 2022 newcomer.quetta-: Jupiter's mass is about 1.9 quettagrams, so the biggest planet in our system fits snugly into this largest SI prefix.

When these leaders were born.Elizabeth I: Born in 1533, she lost her mother Anne Boleyn when she was two, executed on her father's orders.
When these leaders were born.Oliver Cromwell: Leader of Parliament's army and then Lord Protector; after his death, his body was dug up and put on trial in 1661.
When these leaders were born.Louis XIV: His reign lasted 72 years, the longest of any major European monarch; he built Versailles and was called the Sun King.
When these leaders were born.Peter the Great: The tsar stood about two metres tall and travelled incognito across Europe to learn shipbuilding, before founding Saint Petersburg.
When these leaders were born.George Washington: The only US president elected unanimously by the Electoral College, and he did it twice.
When these leaders were born.Napoleon Bonaparte: Napoleon was about average height for his time; the 'short' myth owes something to French inches being longer than English ones.
When these leaders were born.Simón Bolívar: El Libertador helped free Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia, which was named in his honour.
When these leaders were born.Abraham Lincoln: At 6 ft 4 in, the tallest US president; he's also the only one to hold a patent, for a device to lift boats over shoals.
When these leaders were born.Otto von Bismarck: He united Germany in 1871 after three wars and created the first state health insurance and old-age pensions.
When these leaders were born.Vladimir Lenin: He led the 1917 Bolshevik Revolution, and his embalmed body has lain in a Moscow mausoleum since 1924.

Defining moments of modern history.World War I begins: The assassination of an archduke in Sarajevo set it off. Over 9 million soldiers died, and the map of Europe was redrawn.
Defining moments of modern history.Russian Revolution: There were really two revolutions in 1917, one in February and one in October. The second brought Lenin's Bolsheviks to power.
Defining moments of modern history.Wall Street Crash: Panicked selling on Black Tuesday wiped out billions in value. The crash helped lead to the Great Depression.
Defining moments of modern history.World War II begins: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September, and Britain and France declared war two days later. It became the deadliest war in history.
Defining moments of modern history.United Nations founded: It was founded in San Francisco with 51 member states, and now has 193. Its headquarters in New York stands on land donated by Rockefeller.
Defining moments of modern history.Korean War begins: It never ended with a peace treaty, only an armistice in 1953. Technically the two Koreas are still at war.
Defining moments of modern history.JFK assassinated: He was shot in Dallas while riding in an open car. His death united many people around the world in shock.
Defining moments of modern history.First Moon landing: Armstrong and Aldrin walked on the surface while Collins orbited above. About 600 million people watched on TV.
Defining moments of modern history.Berlin Wall falls: The announcement that East Germans could cross was almost a mistake, made by a spokesman. Crowds poured through, and the wall had stood 28 years.
Defining moments of modern history.9/11 attacks: Four hijacked planes changed global security. Airport security and international relations were reshaped around the world.

Cinderella, in story order.Her father remarries: Versions of Cinderella exist worldwide, from an ancient Greek-Egyptian tale of Rhodopis to Perrault's 1697 French telling and the Grimms' German one.
Cinderella, in story order.Invitation to the royal ball: In Perrault's version the royal festivities stretch over two nights, giving Cinderella a second chance to slip away just in time.
Cinderella, in story order.Stepsisters leave for the ball: Her name comes from cinders: in French she is Cendrillon, the girl who sleeps near the hearth ashes.
Cinderella, in story order.Fairy godmother appears: The fairy godmother is Perrault's invention; in the Brothers Grimm's version, a hazel tree growing from her mother's grave helps her instead.
Cinderella, in story order.Pumpkin becomes a coach: The 1950 Disney song Bibbidi-Bobbidi-Boo, sung as the coach appears, was nominated for an Oscar for Best Original Song.
Cinderella, in story order.Dances with the prince: Disney's 1950 Cinderella was a hit that rescued the studio's finances after a lean decade, paving the way for its later classics.
Cinderella, in story order.Clock strikes midnight: Midnight as the deadline is Perrault's touch from 1697, giving the tale one of its most famous ticking-clock moments.
Cinderella, in story order.Loses a glass slipper: A popular but disputed theory says the glass slipper began as a mistranslation of vair, meaning fur, into verre, meaning glass.
Cinderella, in story order.Stepsisters try on the slipper: In the Grimm version the stepsisters cut off a toe and a heel to cram into the slipper, until birds reveal the blood.
Cinderella, in story order.The slipper fits: Shoe-fitting as proof of identity appears across cultures; the Chinese tale of Ye Xian, written down around the 9th century, features a golden shoe.

Top speeds of animals and people.Garden snail: Moving on a trail of slime at around 50 meters per hour, it takes a snail about twenty hours to cover a kilometer.
Top speeds of animals and people.Giant tortoise: They plod, but may live well over a hundred years, with one named Jonathan on Saint Helena thought to be around 190.
Top speeds of animals and people.Human walking: A typical adult strolls at about 5 km/h, and walking at that pace burns roughly the same energy as light cycling.
Top speeds of animals and people.Chicken: Chickens can run about 14 km/h, and they can also fly briefly, though not far, thanks to their heavy bodies and short wings.
Top speeds of animals and people.Usain Bolt: His 9.58 second 100 meters world record from 2009 still stands, and his peak speed in it hit roughly 44 km/h.
Top speeds of animals and people.Grizzly bear: Despite their bulk, grizzlies can sprint as fast as a racehorse over short distances, so you can't outrun one.
Top speeds of animals and people.Ostrich: The fastest bird on land can sustain high speed for a long time, and its two-toed feet are unique among birds.
Top speeds of animals and people.Pronghorn: The fastest land animal in North America can hold high speeds far longer than a cheetah, and evolved to outrun cheetahs now extinct.
Top speeds of animals and people.Cheetah: The fastest land animal can go from zero to about 100 km/h in just a few seconds but only for short bursts.
Top speeds of animals and people.Peregrine falcon (diving): The fastest animal on Earth reaches its top speed during a hunting dive called a stoop, with special nostril cones that help it breathe.
